look_here_first: PURPLETOP: first find a tall perennial with a broad open, often drooping panicle (purple in bloom or tan later). THEN inspect the LOWER SHEATHS: the flattened, overlapping, keeled bases often give the crown a two-sided, compressed appearance (Texas A&M; Flora of North Central Texas). This is a supporting field character, not species-proof. Bare lower panicle branches and pink spikelets also occur in Texas tridens; confirm the true very short hair-fringe ligule and measured glumes/lemma before a final ID.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Poaceae: use growth habit, ligule, panicle architecture, spikelet form, lemma hairs and awns. For this old Tridens complex, panicle openness/color and current genus placement are especially useful.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: By far the tallest and most visibly purple member of this batch. The broad reddish-purple panicle separates it quickly from the narrow white seedhead of T. albescens.
field_sequence: 1. Look at the base: multiple upright culms from a tufted perennial crown, often about 60–180 cm tall, with overlapping somewhat flattened lower sheaths.
2. Pull back a leaf blade and inspect its inner collar: ligule is a SHORT FRINGE OF HAIRS, about 0.5 mm; the collar often has additional hairs. No projecting auricles.
3. Measure a leaf blade where possible: usually 3–10 mm wide, flat and tapering; leaf color or white midrib alone is not proof.
4. Check a mature head: an airy, pyramid-shaped open panicle with branches often bending/drooping at the tips; spikelets often purple or reddish, occasionally yellow.

5. With a hand lens, check multi-flowered spikelets (often about 5–10 mm) rather than the tiny one-flowered spikelets of redtop bentgrass. Note sticky/oily mature panicle branches as supporting, not sole, evidence.
morphology_keys.diagnostic_warning: Purple color is seasonal and shared by other grasses; inspect the hairy ligule and multi-flowered spikelets before assigning this species.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.look_here_first: PURPLETOP: seek a tall perennial tuft with a large open, often nodding panicle, then confirm multi-flowered spikelets and a very short hairy/ciliate collar. Purple pigment and exposed basal branch lengths are NOT exclusive species tests.

measured_key.growth_form: Perennial with firm knotty shortly rhizomatous base; culms approximately 60–180 cm in FNA treatment. Record actual rooted basal crown.
measured_key.ligule_collar: Ligule a very short ciliate membrane or hair fringe, up to about 0.5 mm; collar conspicuously hairy. Do not mistake the longer collar hairs for the true ligule.
measured_key.panicle: Open panicle approximately 15–40 cm, with widely spreading or drooping branches, often naked along lower one-third to one-half; these bare branch bases also occur in T. texanus.
measured_key.spikelet_glumes: Pedicellate spikelets 5–10 mm with commonly 4–8 florets. Two one-veined awnless glumes: lower about 2.5–3 mm, upper about 3.5–4 mm.
measured_key.lemma_palea: Fertile lemmas approximately 3–5 mm, three-veined, two-toothed at tip; fine hairs along veins especially lower portions; midvein may project to about 0.5 mm as a mucro. Palea nearly lemma-length.
measured_key.awns: No true long awns. Minute projecting lemma midvein (to about 0.5 mm) must not be annotated as a long awn.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.local_lookalikes: T. texanus may share pink spikelets and naked lower branch segments but generally has smaller, more flexuous flowering panicle; confirm mature glume/lemma dimensions and nerve hairs. T. albescens has much narrower, contracted, upright panicle; panicle color alone fails.
last_mile_photo_arrow_gaps: Rooted flowering purpletop with intact whole 15–40 cm panicle and ruler; repeat mature tan phase.
Attached leaf collar at 10–20× with mm ruler separately showing short true ligule and surrounding white collar hairs.
One 5–10 mm mature spikelet at 10–20× with separated 2 glumes and 4–8 florets; label glume/lemma only where pixels resolve them.
Dissected 3-veined 3–5 mm lemma, lower nerve hairs and two teeth/mucro at mm scale, compared to T. texanus at same magnification.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Large open, often drooping flowering panicle
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look for a tall perennial tuft and a broadly branched 15–40 cm panicle, often reddish-purple while flowering and tan after maturity. Panels 0–1 show different color phases. Do not identify purpletop by color, sticky branch feel or bare lower panicle branches alone: Texas tridens can share those cues. Archived Bob Harms panel 9 additionally shows attached flowering branchlets; do not infer individual lemma anatomy from it.
field_id_short_tiles.status: VISIBLE HEAD SHAPE; CONNECTED ROOTED PLANT GAP

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK THE FLATTENED BASAL SHEATHS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Look for overlapping, laterally flattened/keeled lower sheaths on the perennial crown
field_id_short_tiles.details: Purpletop often has compressed, keeled and overlapping lower sheaths, producing a two-sided base; Texas A&M and Flora of North Central Texas describe this conspicuous vegetative cue. Culms commonly 60–180 cm and the crown can have short rhizomes. Photograph the intact attached lower sheaths from front and side with centimeter scale; do not infer the shape from distant flowering-head images or dig just to prove rhizomes. Confirm with the open panicle and ripe spikelets because base shape alone is not species-diagnostic.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED BASAL SHEATH CUE — NO ATTACHED BASE PHOTO YET

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE INNER COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.details: Expose the actual inner blade/sheath junction at 10–20×. Go Botany describes a hair-type ligule up to 0.5 mm; a conspicuous fringe of longer white hairs can occur on the collar itself. Do not label longer collar hairs as the ligule or imply that the current gallery has a measured collar macro. Archived Bob Harms panel 7 now supplies a genuine source-labelled collar/ligule-region photograph, but does not independently resolve or measure the tiny free ligule margin.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL COLLAR PHOTO; CALIBRATED LIGULE STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT THE FLORETS
field_id_short_tiles.details: The archived Matt Lavin panel 2 shows a real intact purpletop spikelet with overlapping florets, but not a verified millimeter scale or individual dissected glume/lemma identity. Botanical treatments report spikelets about 5–10 mm with commonly 4–8 florets; count the florets inside ONE ripe spikelet. Bob Harms panel 8 also photographs detached reproductive parts beside a metric reference; organ-by-organ glume/lemma assignments and measurements have not been independently verified.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TWO REAL REPRODUCTIVE PHOTOS; INDIVIDUAL PART VALIDATION PENDING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · TWO GLUMES AND A HAIRY LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published purpletop anatomy: lower 1-veined glume approximately 2.5–3 mm, upper 1-veined glume about 3.5–4 mm. Fertile lemma approximately 3–5 mm, three-veined with hairs along lower portions of veins and a two-toothed apex; the central nerve may project as a minute mucro to ~0.5 mm, NOT a long awn. These values are not measurements from panel 2; separate the organs before arrowing. The archived Bob Harms panel 8 is a real detached-parts photograph with metric reference, not proof that the glume vein counts, lemma hairs, paired teeth or mucro can be resolved. No fine arrows should be added without pixel verification.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL DETACHED-PARTS PHOTO; VEINS/HAIRS/MUCRO NOT CERTIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · COMPARE TEXAS AND WHITE TRIDENS
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 3–4 show white tridens (T. albescens) with contracted crowded heads; panels 5–6 show Texas tridens (T. texanus) with a generally shorter flexuous panicle. Both purpletop and Texas tridens can have exposed proximal branch sections and rosy spikelets. Compare mature glume/lemma lengths and hairy lemma nerves when gross architecture overlaps. Check purpletop's flattened keeled overlapping basal sheaths on the same attached plant as an additional field cue; do not assume this trait alone excludes Texas tridens. When the flowering head is old/tan, verify actual multi-flowered spikelets rather than relying on purple color or sticky branches.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD LOOK-ALIKE CUE; MATCHED MACROS MISSING
